sentences.text: Now keep the same anatomical heart and follow its electrical pathway.
Specialized cells initiate and conduct impulses, and working muscle cells produce force.
Automaticity is spontaneous impulse generation.
Excitability is responding to a stimulus.
Conductivity is transmitting electrical activity.
Contractility is developing force.
These properties are related but not interchangeable.
Electrical activation organizes the sequence of contraction; it does not by itself prove that the heart is pumping effectively.
Find the sinoatrial node, or S A node, high in the right atrium near the superior vena cava.
It is normally the dominant pacemaker.
Its cells depolarize spontaneously, and activity spreads through the atrial muscle.
A usual resting adult sinus rate is sixty to one hundred beats per minute.
This is a clinical teaching range, not a claim that every healthy person's resting rate must fall inside it.
The impulse spreads across both atria and reaches the atrioventricular node, or A V node.
Conduction slows substantially here.
This delay helps coordinate atrial activation with ventricular activation, giving the ventricles time to fill before they contract.
Do not spread this delay evenly along the whole pathway.
After the A V node, the specialized ventricular conduction system is designed for rapid conduction.
From the A V node, the impulse enters the bundle of His, then the right and left bundle branches in the interventricular septum.
Purkinje fibers rapidly distribute activation through the ventricles.
This organization helps the ventricular muscle activate efficiently, with contraction developing from the apex toward the outflow regions.
The colors in the overlay represent the teaching sequence, not the physical color of electricity inside the heart.
If the normal dominant pacemaker slows or impulses fail to reach lower tissue, an escape pacemaker may emerge.
Usual teaching ranges are forty to sixty beats per minute for junctional escape and twenty to forty for ventricular escape.
These are approximate ranges.
Conduction speed and firing rate are different ideas: the A V node conducts slowly, while Purkinje tissue conducts rapidly.
The fastest focus does not always control the heart if conduction is blocked.
Zoom conceptually from the heart to one ventricular muscle cell.
Its action potential begins with rapid sodium entry.
A brief early change is followed by a plateau, during which calcium entry and potassium exit both matter.
Potassium currents then help repolarize the cell.
These changing currents flow through ion channels.
The sodium-potassium pump maintains ion gradients over time; it is not the channel that produces every action-potential upstroke.
Pacemaker cells do not have the same stable resting potential or the same action-potential shape as ventricular working cells.
Their membrane voltage drifts toward threshold, and calcium current contributes to the nodal upstroke.
Threshold and resting values vary by cell type and conditions.
Do not label calcium, sodium, and potassium with voltages as if those were their electrical charges.
An ion's charge and its equilibrium potential are different quantities.
Now connect electricity to force.
Calcium entering a cardiac muscle cell triggers a larger calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, the cell's internal calcium store.
Calcium binds to troponin.
This moves tropomyosin away from actin's binding sites so myosin can interact with actin.
The process is called excitation-contraction coupling.
The electrical signal starts the sequence, but calcium handling and the contractile machinery determine how force develops.
Within a muscle cell, myofibrils contain repeating sarcomeres.
Each sarcomere spans from one Z line to the next.
At the sarcomere, myosin heads bind to actin, produce force, detach, and reset through repeated cross-bridge cycles.
A T P is needed for this cycle, including detachment of myosin from actin.
Thin and thick filaments slide past one another; the filaments themselves do not become shorter.
The distance between the sarcomere boundaries decreases.
Many sarcomeres acting together shorten the muscle cell and contribute to ventricular pressure.
For relaxation, the free calcium concentration in the cell must fall.
Much calcium returns to the sarcoplasmic reticulum through an A T P-dependent pump.
Calcium also leaves the cell, especially through the sodium-calcium exchanger.
As calcium dissociates from troponin, tropomyosin again limits actin-myosin interaction.
The sodium-potassium pump supports the gradients that make this system possible.
Relaxation is an active, energy-dependent process, not simply the absence of an electrical wave.
Ions are atoms or molecules carrying an electrical charge.
Sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium are positive ions; chloride is a negative ion.
Different concentrations inside and outside the cell, together with selective membrane permeability, create electrical and chemical gradients.
The sodium-potassium pump uses A T P to move three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in.
This maintains gradients over time and indirectly supports calcium handling; channels carry the rapid currents of each action potential.

sentences.text: During the refractory period, cardiac muscle cannot respond normally to another stimulus.
Early in recovery, a new propagated response cannot be triggered normally; later, a sufficiently strong premature stimulus may trigger one.
These cellular periods do not have one exact boundary on every surface T wave.
Put the sequence in order: impulse spread, calcium release, cross-bridge force, calcium removal, and relaxation.
Then return to the original heart and trace S A node to Purkinje fibers.
